prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: I keep B022 as my single part. Of the shortlisted candidates, it best meets the standard I stated publicly in 2023: new evidence together with an explanatory account of what drives it. The China-shock studies use transparent quasi-experimental designs on a first-order question, namely who bears the cost when technology and trade change labour demand. They show that adjustment in local labour markets can be slow and costly. The record is about two decades old and has been replicated, re-analysed and contested, so the claim has been tested and is not merely influential. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the joint authors of the central trade-shock papers, so a three-name credit set is accurate for what the citation names. My configuration has changed in one respect since round 1. I have dropped 'and conceptual' from the citation. The chair's question showed that this wording invites the task-model attribution problem, because the originators of that framework (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane) are outside the credited set. The citation should rest on what is attributable: the empirical evidence on labour demand, local adjustment and wage inequality. The names and the ballot are unchanged. I do not rely on the fact that five members now prefer B022. That count is one short of a majority and says nothing about merit. My case rests on the research design, the originality of the question, the replication record and the clarity of credit.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the sensitivity of shift-share designs, remain contested. I cannot settle that from the supplied evidence. As far as I can judge, the dispute concerns how large and how lasting the effects are, and not whether adjustment costs exist. The prize could also be read as rewarding a research design and measurement programme more than a conceptual advance. The theme is close to the 2024 prize on technology and institutions. Narrowing the citation to the empirical evidence leaves the task framework's other originators unrecognised, and I accept that cost. A fair-minded member could reasonably weigh B012's longer confirmation record and cleaner two-name attribution more heavily than I do. B014 may well prove the stronger discovery in time.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B012 and judges firm heterogeneity to have the broader and better-confirmed reach. He ranks B014 seventh because its core results are recent, the causal reading of neighbourhood effects is still under scrutiny, and credit is spread over a large team.
responses.response: I accept his maturity argument on B014. It is why I moved that ballot from first place to an alternative in round 1, and I have not reversed it. I still see it as sequencing and not a weakness of substance. On B012 versus B022, I do not think breadth of confirmed use in trade theory and firm microdata settles the comparison. Both are strong on the common criteria. B022 is the more direct evidence on how shocks redistribute income across people and places, a question the heterogeneous-firm framework does not address. I would not oppose B012, because its attribution is clean. For me the deciding points are the strength of the identification and the size of the distributional finding.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B012 with Melitz and Helpman. He regards the research designs in B022 as credible and the policy relevance as large, but he notes that the task framework has origins outside the credited set and that the persistence of the China-shock effects is contested.
responses.response: I share both reservations and have tried to meet them in the citation. I have removed the 'conceptual' claim, so that it covers only the empirical analysis of technology and import competition and does not assert the task framework. I would answer the persistence point as I did with Hassler: the debate is about magnitude and duration, and the Scientific Background should address the re-analyses directly. I agree that adding Dorn or Katz is a real judgement call. I keep Dorn because he is a co-author of the core China-shock papers. Boppart also calls B022 his first alternative, and I treat that as an argument about its content, not as a vote. My own view is that B012 is strong and that B022 is the stronger fit to the data-plus-framework standard.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B022 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. She notes that B014 is about a decade old, that the causal reading of neighbourhood effects is still being tested, and that credit within its team is hard to divide, since she had to leave Friedman and Katz out of her own pair.
responses.response: I agree on the three names and on the exclusion of Katz, whose claims sit in the earlier skill-premium work and in B014. On B014 I accept her team-attribution point. In my own opening I named Chetty, Hendren and Friedman, and that triple already leaves out contested contributors such as Katz. I would add that B014 is better described as new population-scale data combined with modern causal design than as measurement alone, so a future citation would need to name the causal findings. My difference with her is small: I think B014 is close to ready, and she thinks it may become stronger in a few years. Neither of us has evidence to settle that now.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B022 with three names. He argues that B012 and B022 do not compete for the same ground, because B012 concerns trade theory and quantification while B022 concerns the distributional and labour-market consequences of trade and technology shocks.
responses.response: I agree that the two cover different ground, but I draw a more modest conclusion. The Committee still has to choose between them, so they have to be compared on the common criteria of originality, breadth of confirmation and attributable credit. I think B012 scores higher on clean attribution and long confirmation, and B022 scores higher on identification and on the size of the finding about people and places. I also share his view that the citation should be tied to the empirical evidence on labour demand and adjustment, not to task-model theory. On the 2024 proximity, I read B022 as a distinct finding, though I accept that it is a judgement about timing and not a verdict on merit.

uncertainties: How far the China-shock magnitudes and persistence survive re-analyses and shift-share identification critiques. I cannot settle this from the supplied evidence.
Whether a citation limited to the empirical evidence can be worded to avoid implying credit for the task framework, whose other originators are outside the credited set.
Whether the 2024 prize's thematic proximity is a reason for delay or only a timing judgement, and whether other members read it as bearing on merit.
Whether B012 should rank above B022 on the common criteria. I find this close and judgement-dependent.
Whether B014's recency is a real scientific reservation or only a sequencing issue, and who should be named if it is pursued.
My attribution views rest on the supplied evidence and general knowledge. I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile for B022 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) or for the alternatives B014 and B012. My listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not among the credited names on those ballots. My research on labour economics, crime and inequality, including the ERC grant on the 'inequality-crime cycle', is adjacent to B014 and B022. I treat that as subject expertise and not as merit or a tie to any candidate. I presented the 2023 prize at the announcement, which creates no link to a 2026 candidate. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
